strengths: The paper presents a coherent, mechanistically-informed pipeline (circuit discovery → channel-wise activation scaling → preventative fine-tuning) that is clearly described and reasonably well-motivated.

Evaluation is multi-faceted: three different LLM families, multiple baselines including recent SoTA mechanistic defenses (Circuit Breaker, RepBend), and a safety-utility trade-off analysis with an explicitly defined Pareto/Overall metric.

The in-depth analysis is a genuine strength: ablation of identified heads vs. random heads, linear probe verification of tense encoding in the identified heads, dot-product distribution analysis, and circuit reconstruction after defense to show the vulnerability circuit was altered rather than merely patched.
The comparison against Sahara (Zhou et al., 2025) in the appendix usefully differentiates attack-specific 'vulnerable heads' from general safety heads, supporting the paper's positioning.

The preventative fine-tuning idea (train with the vulnerability neutralized, then remove the intervention) is a plausible and interesting mechanism for avoiding the brittleness of post-hoc suppression.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is largely a combination of existing techniques — EAP-IG circuit discovery (Nanda, Hanna et al.), activation scaling (Lee et al., 2025; Stoehr et al., 2024), and preventative-style fine-tuning inspired by Chen et al. (2025) — applied to a single known attack. The authors themselves acknowledge these prior components; the contribution is integration, not a new method or new scientific insight.

Narrow scope: the defense is designed and evaluated only against tense jailbreaking. There is no evaluation of generalization to other semantic reformulation attacks, adaptive attacks, or an adaptive attacker aware of the defense, so the central security claim is only weakly supported. Meanwhile SFT and Circuit Breaker achieve 0% ASR on this attack, so ASGUARD's residual 8–19% ASR needs stronger justification.

Fragile methodology: head identification depends on hand-tuned thresholds (τ between 0.1 and 0.03), specific clean/corrupted run construction, and the False-to-True vs. Always-False filtering; sensitivity of results to these choices is not analyzed.

Only-scaling results show the core intervention can severely damage capability (Gemma2 MMLU drops from 72.2 to 50.3), and the mechanism by which preventative fine-tuning repairs this is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Statistical rigor is lacking: no error bars, seeds, or repeated runs for any experiment; judge-based ASR (GPT-4.1) with no human verification; linear probe accuracy (73–77%) is described as 'high' but is only moderately above chance and could partly reflect token-frequency or length artifacts.

The composite 'Overall' and 'R-Score' metrics are self-defined and normalize in ways that can favor the proposed method; some table entries appear erroneous or garbled (e.g., Gemma2 'Only Scaling' R-Score of 5.92 and Overall of 8.96), undermining confidence in the reported numbers.

Presentation issues: captions of Figures 5 and 6 are copy-pasted from Figure 3 and incorrectly reference Llama3.1 and head L13H25; there are numerous grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'pople', 'acheives', 'faled') throughout, and the linear probe 'accuracy change' arrows are inconsistently signed/interpreted.

Missing ablations on the preventative fine-tuning stage itself (e.g., over-scaled vectors, number of epochs, effect of detaching), and no discussion of why identified heads differ so drastically across models relative to Temporal Heads beyond speculation.

strengths: The paper is one of the first attempts to connect circuit-level analysis (EAP-IG) to a concrete defense for a specific semantic jailbreak (past-tense rephrasing), and the identify-then-scale + preventative fine-tuning pipeline is a reasonable and well-motivated design.

Evaluation covers three LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) and includes a reasonable set of baselines (SFT with different mixture ratios, DPO, Circuit Breaker, RepBend) across targeted ASR, general refusal, over-refusal, and MMLU.

The ablation tests, linear probe analysis, and post-ASGUARD circuit reconstruction (Section 6) go beyond a black-box defense paper and provide supporting mechanistic evidence for the identified heads.
The 'Only Scaling' vs. full ASGUARD comparison on Gemma-2 (MMLU 50.3 vs 72.2) convincingly demonstrates that the preventative fine-tuning stage contributes beyond naive intervention.
Hyperparameters, prompts, judge configuration, and dataset construction are documented in the appendix, and code/data are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Narrow scope and significance: the method is designed for and evaluated on exactly one attack family (past-tense rephrasing of JBB-Behaviors). There is no evaluation of cross-attack generalization (GCG, PAIR, paraphrase, other semantic manipulations) or against an adaptive attacker, so the practical value of 'surgically patching' this single vulnerability is unclear. This is acknowledged only obliquely in limitations.

The headline 'Pareto-optimal' claim rests on a self-defined composite metric (Overall = mean of ASR reduction and R-Score, Appendix A.3) rather than a standard, validated measure; conclusions about the safety-utility frontier are sensitive to this metric design. Notably, SFT (30/70) on Qwen achieves 0% ASR and second-best Overall, which the paper dismisses narratively rather than metrically.

Evaluation relies entirely on GPT-4.1 as judge with 100 base prompts (and 20 reformulations each); no human verification, no variance across seeds, and no statistical significance testing. Reported ASR differences of a few percentage points (e.g., 8% vs 13%, or 19% vs 26%) may not be reliable.

Anomalous/inconsistent numbers undermine confidence: in Table 2, 'Only Scaling' on Gemma shows R-Score 5.92 and Overall 8.96 (clearly formatting errors breaking the 0-100 scale of every other row), and the R-Score/Overall columns are undefined for base models. Figure 5 and 6 captions are copy-pasted from Figure 3 and reference 'Llama3.1' and head 'L13H25' for Qwen and Gemma results.

Novelty is limited: each ingredient is established (EAP-IG circuit discovery, channel-wise activation scaling following Lee et al. 2025 and Stoehr et al. 2024, fine-tuning during guided/steered states following Chen et al. 2025); the contribution is essentially their combination applied to one attack, and the paper itself frames the scaling vector as an extension of prior verified work.

The mechanistic story is weaker than claimed: several 'tense vulnerable' heads have near-chance linear probe accuracy (e.g., L0H3 at ~0.3 in Figure 3, L26H27 at ~0.2 in Figure 5), and the identified head sets are model-specific with no consistent pattern; the causal narrative in Section 6.1 ('signals downstream safety mechanisms that the query is a historical inquiry') is speculative and not directly validated.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: multiple typos in the main text ('pople', 'acheives', 'lists up', 'faled', 'epcoh'), grammatical issues throughout, and Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse. Writing issues suggest insufficient polish.

The circuit analysis step adds substantial pipeline complexity (corrupted/clean runs, 5 refusal prompt variants, threshold tuning 0.1-0.03) whose contribution relative to simply fine-tuning on refusal data at the identified layers is not ablated.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete, well-motivated vulnerability (tense jailbreaking) and connects it to a mechanistic account, using EAP-IG circuit analysis to localize 'tense vulnerable heads' and verifying them with causal ablation and linear probe classification — a solid, falsifiable pipeline.

The proposed method is composed into a sensible three-stage framework (circuit identification → channel-wise scaling → preventative fine-tuning), with the fine-tuning stage plausibly explaining why the standalone scaling baseline damages MMLU on Gemma while ASGUARD does not.

Evaluation spans three model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) and includes a reasonably broad baseline set (SFT with two data mixes, DPO, Circuit Breaker, RepBend) plus complementary axes of utility (OR-Bench-Toxic/Hard, MMLU), not just attack success rate.

Section 6/Appendix A.4 provides genuinely interesting post-hoc analysis: reconstructing circuits after ASGUARD, showing heads are re-weighted rather than deleted, and comparing against the Sahara head-attribution method to argue that attack-specific (vs. global) safety mechanisms are distinguishable.
Code and data are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: each component is borrowed from prior work — EAP-IG circuits (Nanda, Hanna et al.), channel-wise activation scaling (Lee et al., Stoehr et al.), and preventative/steering-during-training regularization (Chen et al.). The contribution is a combination applied to one specific attack, and the paper itself concedes Lee et al. 'already verified the effectiveness of the light-weight scaling vector.'

The headline claims are not consistently supported by Table 2. On Gemma-2-9B, ASGUARD achieves Overall 44.6, which is below SFT (5/95) at 48.3, and ASR only drops 38→19 — contradicting the abstract's claim of a 'Pareto-optimal balance' and 'consistently operates on the Pareto-optimal frontier.' The Pareto narrative is partly an artifact of the authors' custom R-Score/Overall metrics (A.3), which are ad hoc equal-weight aggregates and not established evaluation measures.

The causal attribution is weaker than claimed. Ablating all identified vulnerable heads reduces ASR by only 4–13 pp, so the heads are implicated but clearly not sufficient for the jailbreak; language like 'causally linked' and 'surgically mitigates' overstates the mechanistic certainty, and the later admission that 'intervening only on the heads most responsive to tense is less effective' partially undercuts the paper's own localization story.

The defense is evaluated only against the fixed tense-jailbreak attack with a single judge model (GPT-4.1) and no variance/significance reporting. There is no adaptive-attack evaluation (a standard expectation for safety defenses), no testing against other jailbreak families to check generalization, and the training/eval prompts both come from JBB-Behaviors, raising contamination/overfitting concerns given only 100 base prompts × 20 reformulations.

Evidence of internal inconsistency in the claims: ASGUARD substantially increases OR-Bench-Hard over-refusal (28.9→66.8 on Llama; 70.5→88.0 on Gemma), which is difficult to reconcile with the abstract's 'minimizing over refusal.' The Gemma 'Only Scaling' row also contains apparent typos (R-Score 5.92, Overall 8.96), and Figures 5–6 have captions copy-pasted from the Llama analysis (referencing head L13H25 and 'Llama3.1'), suggesting insufficient care in presentation.

Writing quality is below top-venue standards: numerous grammatical errors ('acheives', 'list up', 'epcoh', 'faled', 'COMPARISION', 'propriety of our approach'), inconsistent notation (τ 'is various between 0.1 to 0.03'), and threshold/hyperparameter choices (ig-step, top-n, τ ranges, per-model learning rates) are reported but not justified or ablated — the sensitivity of circuit discovery to τ in particular could change the entire identified head list.

Generalizability is admittedly narrow (conclusion and A.4.1 concede the approach does not transfer well: Phi-3-mini is 'too sensitive,' distilled/MoE models behave differently, and for Qwen/Gemma only one or two heads show probe-accuracy gains). This limits the impact of the method beyond the specific Llama-style setting.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and specific problem (tense jailbreaking) with a mechanistically grounded defense pipeline: EAP-IG-based circuit discovery to localize 'tense vulnerable' attention heads, channel-wise activation scaling, and a preventative fine-tuning stage that trains the model while the intervention is active, then detaches it. This is a coherent and sensible overall design.

Evaluation is comparatively broad: four open-source LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2-7B), targeted ASR on past-tense jailbreaks plus two OOD attacks (GCG, LogiBreak), general safety (OR-Bench-Toxic), over-refusal (OR-Bench-Hard), and general capability (MMLU).

Reasonable set of baselines (SFT with two mix ratios, DPO, RepE, Circuit Breaker, RepBend, head ablation, scaling-only), and the paper honestly reports failure modes of baselines (e.g., SFT inducing 98.5% over-refusal on Qwen2.5 or MMLU collapse on Gemma2).

Good control experiments: random-head ablation, random scaling, random PFT (Appendix A.3, Table 4) showing circuit-targeted intervention beats arbitrary head suppression, plus linear probe / dot-product analyses that corroborate the tense-encoding role of identified heads, and post-hoc circuit reconstruction after ASGUARD (§6.2).

Clear Pareto-frontier framing of the safety-utility trade-off, with a composite Overall score and R-Score defined explicitly in A.4, and hyperparameter details sufficient for approximate reproduction; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each component is an adaptation of existing techniques (EAP-IG circuit discovery, activation/channel scaling following Stoehr et al./Lee et al., and preventative fine-tuning explicitly 'inspired by Chen et al., 2025'). The contribution is primarily an integration and application to tense jailbreaks rather than a new method or new scientific insight.

Evaluation scale and statistical rigor are weak: circuit discovery uses only 100 JBB prompts with 20 reformulations each; all results appear to be single runs with no seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing; jailbreak success is judged solely by GPT-4.1 without human verification, and the same LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo) generates the attack reformulations.

The Overall metric is ad hoc (simple mean of ASRpp and R-Score) and appears constructed to favor the proposed method; 'Pareto-optimal' claims rest partly on this self-defined composite rather than a strict dominance argument.

The headline OOD result is underexplained and suspicious: scaling heads discovered on tense circuits reduces GCG ASR from 15 to 1 and LogiBreak ASR from 30 to 13, a very strong cross-attack generalization that contradicts the paper's own circuit-specificity narrative and is not analyzed mechanistically; conversely the LogiBreak improvement is modest relative to claims.

Method fragility and model dependence are evident: 'Only Scaling' collapses MMLU on Gemma2 (72.2 to 50.3), ASGUARD only reaches 19% ASR on Gemma2 (vs. 8-9% elsewhere), and linear-probe improvements after fine-tuning hold only for Llama3.1, not Qwen2.5/Gemma2 (A.5.1). The authors acknowledge sensitivity in the limitations but this weakens the 'across four LLMs' generality claim.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: typos ('pople', 'acheives', 'epcoh', 'comparision'), grammatical errors, an apparent typo listing 'ASGuard' as a baseline in A.3, odd R-Score value (5.92) in Table 1, and an undefined/jargon-heavy description of circuit construction thresholds (tau varying 0.1-0.03 without justification).

Circuit identification relies on contrasting success vs. failure attack cases, which introduces potential selection bias; the paper does not quantify faithfulness of the discovered circuits beyond generic EAP-IG faithfulness checks, and the per-model head lists are not validated for stability across attack samples.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and timely problem: repairing a specific, well-documented alignment vulnerability (tense jailbreaking) rather than applying blanket safety training.

The overall pipeline is reasonably complete: circuit discovery (EAP-IG), targeted channel-wise activation scaling, and a preventative fine-tuning stage, with each stage ablated (Head Ablation, Only Scaling, full ASGUARD).
Evaluation covers four LLM families and multiple axes (targeted ASR, general refusal, over-refusal, MMLU), and includes additional attack types (GCG, LogiBreak) for out-of-domain robustness.

The random-head control analysis (Table 4) is a useful sanity check that circuit-guided head selection is doing non-trivial work, and the linear probe analysis provides some mechanistic verification of the identified heads.
Reproducibility statement and detailed hyperparameters in the appendix are provided.
weaknesses: Central claims are stronger than the evidence. The claim of 'Pareto-optimal balance' and 'outperforming SFT, DPO and other representation intervention' is contradicted by the paper's own results: on Gemma2, SFT(5/95) achieves Overall 48.3 vs ASGUARD's 44.6, and on Qwen2.5, SFT(30/70) achieves 58.7 vs ASGUARD's 58.8. Several baselines reach 0–3% ASR versus ASGUARD's 8–19%. The Pareto-optimality narrative does not hold uniformly.

The proposed 'Overall' metric (mean of ASRpp and R-Score, Eq. 12–13) is ad hoc, not validated, and produces questionable rankings (e.g., an SFT variant that drops MMLU from 72.2 to 43.1 still ranks above ASGUARD). Conclusions built on this custom metric are fragile.

Novelty is limited: each component is borrowed and lightly adapted — EAP-IG circuit discovery (Nanda, Hanna et al.), channel-wise scaling vectors (Lee et al., 2025, explicitly acknowledged), and preventative fine-tuning (Chen et al., 2025, explicitly acknowledged as inspiration). The paper is essentially a combination of existing techniques applied to one specific attack.

Scope of the defense is narrow: it targets a single attack family (past-tense rephrasing). The OOD generalization argument rests on only two additional attacks and is tested only on Llama-3.1, and tense-specific scaling does not obviously guard against the broader space of semantic jailbreaks. Adaptive attacks are not considered at all.

Small and noisy evaluation: 100 jailbreaking prompts with 20 reformulations, a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with no human validation or agreement analysis, and no variance/significance reporting. Differences such as 9% vs 8% ASR or Overall 58.7 vs 58.8 are presented as meaningful without statistical support.

Unexplained anomalous results undermine technical soundness: 'Only Scaling' on Gemma2 collapses (MMLU 50.3, R-Score 5.92, Overall 8.96), yet no explanation or mitigation is given; results on non-Llama models are notably weaker, and the mechanism narrative (tense-detection heads) is supported by probe accuracies of only ~73–76%.

Writing quality is poor and distracts from the contribution: numerous grammatical errors ('pople', 'acheives', 'list up', 'epcoh', 'refer the accuracy change'), awkward phrasing throughout, typos in figure references, and formatting issues (empty footnote URL on page 1).

Circuit analysis results are not rigorously validated: threshold τ is hand-varied between 0.03–0.1 per case, and the identified 'vulnerable heads' (Table 3) differ entirely across models with no theoretical account of why; the claimed distinction from Temporal Heads is interesting but under-analyzed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper connects a documented, concrete alignment failure (tense jailbreaking, Andriushchenko & Flammarion 2025) to a mechanistic account, and then builds a defense from that account — the 'identify-then-scale' pipeline is a coherent and sensible use of mechanistic interpretability for safety.

Comprehensive experimental design: four instruction-tuned LLMs from different families, three attack families (tense, GCG, LogiBreak), and a multi-facet evaluation covering targeted ASR, general safety (OR-Bench-Toxic), over-refusal (OR-Bench-Hard), and general capability (MMLU), with a Pareto-frontier analysis (Figure 2).
Appropriate and recent baselines (SFT at two mix ratios, DPO, RepE, Circuit Breaker, RepBend) re-run under a unified pipeline and judge, which makes the relative comparisons fair.

Good ablation and control experiments: naive head ablation, random-head scaling and random-head preventative fine-tuning (Table 4) convincingly show the gains are not from suppressing arbitrary heads; the 'Only Scaling' vs. full ASGUARD ablation isolates the contribution of preventative fine-tuning.

Mechanistic verification beyond headline numbers: linear probes per vulnerable head, dot-product distribution analysis, post-ASGUARD circuit reconstruction (§6.2), and comparison with Sahara (A.5.2) substantiate the causal story rather than only claiming it.
Parameter efficiency and deployability: channel-wise scaling can be fused into W_O at no inference cost, and the scaling vectors are detached after preventative fine-tuning.
Reproducibility statement with code, detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and judge instructions in the appendix.
weaknesses: Narrow attack scope for the main results: the circuit identification, scaling vectors, and fine-tuning are tailored to the tense jailbreak, and the OOD experiments (GCG, LogiBreak) are only run on Llama-3.1. There is no evidence the pipeline generalizes across attack types on the other three models, and no adaptive-attack evaluation (an adversary aware of the defense could look for other circuits/attacks).

Novelty is somewhat incremental: channel-wise head scaling builds on Lee et al. (2025)/Stoehr et al. (2024), and preventative fine-tuning is explicitly inspired by Chen et al. (2025); the primary new contribution is the circuit-guided localization plus their combination, which is a solid but not groundbreaking synthesis.

Evaluation scale and statistical rigor are limited: circuit discovery uses only 100 JBB-Behaviors prompts with 20 reformulations each, training sets are small (1k–5k), and no variance, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results are reported for ASR or the benchmark scores.

The custom 'Overall' metric (A.4) is ad hoc: it averages ASR reduction in percentage points with a normalized R-Score, giving unequal weighting to arbitrary scales; conclusions of 'Pareto-optimality' partly rest on this constructed metric rather than the raw benchmarks alone. There are also presentation inconsistencies (e.g., LogiBreak ASR reported as 13 in Table 2 but 15% in §5.3/abstract; R-Score 5.92/Overall 8.96 formatting for 'Only Scaling' on Gemma2).

Writing quality issues: numerous typos and grammatical problems ('pople', 'epcoh', 'list up', 'acheives', 'We also simplify each circuits'), which detract from polish and occasionally create ambiguity (e.g., the description of clean/corrupted runs in §3.1).
Only GPT-4.1 is used as the semantic judge; no human validation or second-judge agreement is reported, which matters for jailbreak ASR claims.

Practical applicability constraints are acknowledged but underexplored: the method requires white-box access, per-attack circuit discovery per model, and the authors themselves note fragility on smaller models (Phi-3-mini) and possibly on distilled/MoE architectures; the cost of the full EAP-IG pipeline is not quantified.

Some mechanistic claims are asserted more strongly than the evidence supports (e.g., the narrative that tense heads 'signal to downstream safety mechanisms that the query is a historical inquiry' is plausible but only indirectly supported by probe accuracies of ~73–77%).
